name: Linearize A Generic Tree - Efficient Approach
html:
Welcome back, dear reader. So we hope that you have already solved this problem LINEARIZE A GENERIC TREE. We request you to solve this problem first and also watch the solution video or read the LINEARIZE A GENERIC TREE ARTICLE so that you get familiar with the previous method as in this article, we are going to discuss the efficient approach for the same.

Important Links : Problem Link, Question Video, Solution Video

Problem Discussion :

So, the question is to linearize a generic tree. What do we mean by this? Have a look at the diagram shown below:

A generic tree and its linear version is shown in the above diagram. We have linearized this tree on the basis of the preorder traversal. If you start from the root and write down all the values of the nodes in the linearized version of the tree, you will get the preorder traversal of this tree.

You may also refer to the question video for the LINEARIZE A GENERIC TREE problem to understand the problem if you have any doubts about it. Also, we hope that you are clear with the pre-order traversal of a generic tree and know what it is and how to traverse a tree in its pre order. You may refer here if you want to know about the pre-order traversal of a tree.

Watch video Approach : Recapitulating the Previous Approach:

Let us have a quick recap of the approach discussed in the previous problem. If you want to understand this approach in detail, you may refer to the LINEARIZE A GENERIC TREE SOLUTION VIDEO or the LINEARIZE A GENERIC TREE ARTICLE as here we will just have a quick recap of it.

Watch video

High-level Thinking:

Expectation : Our expectation is clear that we have to linearize a generic tree in its pre-order fashion. (Have a look at fig-1)

Faith and Relation: Let us assume that our problem is a big problem and let's try to break it down into smaller ones. So, we can have a faith that recursion will linearize the sub-trees that emerge from the root node. (Have a look at fig-2)

As shown in the diagram, we have a faith that the children of the root node will get linearized on calling the function upon the root node. Now, what do we have to do to linearize this entire tree? Have a look at the diagrams shown below:

We removed the last child of the root node and added it to the children arrayList of the tail of the second last child of the root node (fig-3 (a)). Next, we again removed the last node and added it to the children of the tail of the second last node. We repeat this until only one child node of the root node is remaining.

So, this is the procedure that we can apply. Now the question is how can we know about the tail of the last child node.

Determining the Tail:

Have a look at the diagram given below:

Let us say, we have separated the last child node of the root node from it. Now, we want to find the tail of the second last node. So, we have a Node type of variable t on the second last child node of the root node as shown in the figure. Now, if we observe carefully, there is only one child node of this node i.e. node (70). (Look at fig-4). Similarly, node (70) also has only one child node and all the further nodes have only one child node because we have linearized this part of the tree (recursion faith). So, only the last node i.e. the tail of the node t is the only node with no child. So, we can do this:

Move t to the child node of t until there comes the leaf node i.e. until we encounter a node that has no child node. So, stop at that node and return it. This will be the tail.

So, this is the entire procedure that we learnt previously. Again, this is just a short and quick explanation for this method. If you have any doubts regarding this method, you may refer to the solution video for this method.

Watch video Complexity Analysis of previous approach:

Let us try to find out the time and space complexity of this method and then optimize our approach:

Space Complexity: The space complexity is O(1) as we have not used any extra space.

Time Complexity: We have visited every node to linearize it. Although the leaf nodes do not get linearized, still we have visited them and so, we have visited n nodes. Also, when we visit them and try to linearize them, we visit all the nodes after linearizing in order to find the tail and add the next node in the pre-order to its children arraylist. This happens inside the first loop of traversal. So, in a way- we have a nested loop where we are visiting almost n elements every time. So, the time complexity is O(n2).

So, dear reader, if you have any doubts about the time and space complexity analysis you may refer to the solution video for LINEARIZE A GENERIC TREE-EFFICIENT APPROACH. Now that we know that this solution is having an O(n2) complexity, we understand the need to optimize it. So, let's move to the optimization part now.

Watch video Efficient Approach:

If we try to think about reducing the complexity of the above method, we can say that the time complexity was increasing because of the returnTail(node) method as it had to traverse a lot and then return the tail. So, let us try to avoid this traversal. What can we do about that? Think!!!

Change in Faith:

Let's now modify the faith that we had at recursion previously. Earlier, we had a faith that the recursion will linearize the child nodes of the root node. Now, let us say that the recursion will linearize the child nodes of the root node and also return the tail of that child node.

What do we mean by this? Have a look at the diagram shown below:

In this diagram, we have shown that when we linearize the last child node of the root node, we get back the tail of the last child node. Now, when we linearize the next child node and remove this, we will get its tail. That tail can store the last child node into its children arrayList and we won't have to traverse the entire chain for finding the tail. (Have a look at fig-6)

So, what are the steps that we are following?

  1. We linearised the last child node and got its tail as the function returns the tail of the node being linearised.
  2. Next, we removed this node from the children arraylist of the root node (we obviously stord it in a variable before removing it).
  3. Lastly, we linearised the second last child node. Since we linearised it, we got the tail of this node. So, we add the last node which was removed from the children of the root node as the child to this tail. (see fig-6)
  4. This will repeat until the size of the children arraylist of the root node becomes 1. This is because when it becomes 1, the root will be connected to only one child and so will be all the other nodes in the tree except the last node (which will be the tail of the overall linearised tree). (see fig-7)

Base Case: Since we are repeating this procedure till the size of the children arraylist of the node is greater than 1, what if the size is zero? Just think, which node will have the size of children arraylist equal to 0. Well it is simple, the node with no children. So basically, the leaf node is where we can encounter a problem. If you think, we do not need to linearize the leaf node as there is no child node for it and it is already linearized. Also, the leaf node itself is a tail. Therefore, whenever we encounter any leaf node, we will simply return it and this will be our base case.

So, dear reader, if you have any doubts regarding this method, you may refer to the solution video to understand the concept completely. So, that's it my friend. That's all we have to do. Isn't it simpler than the previous method also? I guess it is. Now that we have understood the complete procedure, let's move to the code.

Watch video Pseudo Code

You have already done the linearize a generic tree problem. So, the approach is going to be similar. We are going to use recursion to solve this problem.

  1. High level Thinking: In the high level thinking we have established a faith that if we call the function linearize(node) for the children of the root node then they will be linearized and will return their tail respectively.
  2. Joining the tail: Since the tail gets returned to us, we will remove the last child node and in the tail of the second last child node, we will add the last child node as its child.
  3. Low-Level Thinking: On applying the low-level thinking, we can understand the base case of the recursion. We have to return whenever we get a leaf node as it has no children. The tail of a leaf node is itself the leaf node itself and we cannot linearize it.
import java.io.*; import java.util.*; public class Main { private static class Node { int data; ArrayList< Node> children = new ArrayList< >(); } public static void display(Node node) { String str = node.data + " -> "; for (Node child : node.children) { str += child.data + ", "; } str += "."; System.out.println(str); for (Node child : node.children) { display(child); } } public static Node construct(int[] arr) { Node root = null; Stack< Node> st = new Stack< >(); for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { if (arr[i] == -1) { st.pop(); } else { Node t = new Node(); t.data = arr[i]; if (st.size() > 0) { st.peek().children.add(t); } else { root = t; } st.push(t); } } return root; } public static int size(Node node) { int s = 0; for (Node child : node.children) { s += size(child); } s += 1; return s; } public static int max(Node node) { int m = Integer.MIN_VALUE; for (Node child : node.children) { int cm = max(child); m = Math.max(m, cm); } m = Math.max(m, node.data); return m; } public static int height(Node node) { int h = -1; for (Node child : node.children) { int ch = height(child); h = Math.max(h, ch); } h += 1; return h; } public static void traversals(Node node) { System.out.println("Node Pre " + node.data); for (Node child : node.children) { System.out.println("Edge Pre " + node.data + "--" + child.data); traversals(child); System.out.println("Edge Post " + node.data + "--" + child.data); } System.out.println("Node Post " + node.data); } public static void levelOrderLinewiseZZ(Node node) { Stack< Node> stack = new Stack< >(); stack.add(node); Stack< Node> cstack = new Stack< >(); int level = 0; while (stack.size() > 0) { node = stack.pop(); System.out.print(node.data + " "); if (level % 2 == 0) { for (int i = 0; i < node.children.size(); i++) { Node child = node.children.get(i); cstack.push(child); } } else { for (int i = node.children.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Node child = node.children.get(i); cstack.push(child); } } if (stack.size() == 0) { stack = cstack; cstack = new Stack< >(); level++; System.out.println(); } } } public static void mirror(Node node) { for (Node child : node.children) { mirror(child); } Collections.reverse(node.children); } public static void removeLeaves(Node node) { for (int i = node.children.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Node child = node.children.get(i); if (child.children.size() == 0) { node.children.remove(i); } } for(Node child: node.children){ removeLeaves(child); } } public static Node linearize(Node node){ if(node.children.size()==0) { return node; } Node lkt=linearize(node.children.get(node.children.size()-1)); while(node.children.size()>1) { Node last=node.children.remove(node.children.size()-1); Node sl=node.children.get(node.children.size()-1); Node slt=linearize(sl); slt.children.add(last); } return lkt; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); int[] arr = new int[n]; String[] values = br.readLine().split(" "); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { arr[i] = Integer.parseInt(values[i]); } Node root = construct(arr); linearize(root); display(root); } }
java; true";

So, dear reader, if you have any doubts regarding the code, you may refer to the complete solution video to understand the code with the procedure.

Watch video Analysis: Time Complexity:

The time complexity will be O(n) as this time we are not traversing the nodes to get the tail rather it is returned to us by recursion only.

Space Complexity:

The space complexity is O(1) as we have not used any extra data structure.



We hope that you understood the problem well and got the difference between the two approaches and why our approach that we optimized is the better one. With this, we have completed this problem.

Suggestions:

Here are some suggestions from our side that you do not want to miss:

  1. We suggest that you code the previous method and this method once again by yourself and compare, not only the time complexity but also compare which code is easier for you to understand and implement. We hope that you find the optimized method easy also as compared to the previous method.
  2. Understanding the recursion is really important. We suggest you draw the Euler diagram and try to understand by yourself how the code is working and producing the required results for us. Till then, keep practicing and working hard. Happy Coding!!!!
